Once again, we observed a high degree of variability in the methods employed, such as in the type and number of emotional stimuli, or in the instructions provided to the participants.

Most studies have used affective pictures (e.g., Berman et al., 2022; Huggins et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2017), whereas less commonly used stimuli are autobiographical recalls (Edwards et al., 2020; Edwards & Wupperman, 2017; Fogarty et al., 2015; Grossmann et al., 2016; Mikkelsen et al., 2021), scenarios (Boden et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013; Erbas et al., 2014; Jones & Herr, 2018; Vedernikova et al., 2021), affective movie clips (Aaron et al., 2018; Erbas et al., 2015; Potthoff et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021), pictures combined with news headlines (Jeong et al., 2023), visual art images (Fayn et al., 2018), decision-making trials (Li & Ashkanasy, 2019), and tasks involving naming and rating target persons (Erbas et al., 2014). More broadly, we can distinguish between tasks involving immediate responses to emotion evocative stimuli (e.g., affective pictures or movie clips) and tasks that prompt reflection on past autobiographical events.

In approximately half of the studies, participants were presented with both positive and negative emotional stimuli, whereas the remaining studies used either positive or negative stimuli (or it was not possible to determine emotional valence in advance). The number of stimuli ranged from 6-50 when both positive and negative stimuli were included and from 10-34 in studies focusing on either positive or negative valence.

The instructions provided to participants also varied considerably, even within groups of studies employing the same type of stimuli. For example, concerning autobiographical recall, studies have used different recall cues, asking participants to recall the past events in which they experienced an instance of a specific emotion family or using a predefined list of situations and, for each situation or event, asking the participants to recall their most recent experience. In contrast, other studies have asked participants to recall negative, neutral or positive life events without any further specification. The sum of the total number of studies employing each measurement approach (N) exceeds the total number of studies included in the review (i.e., 115 studies) because some studies assessed emotion differentiation both via ecological and non-ecological methods. "Episodes" refers to the number of emotional episodes reconstructed each day. "Prompts" refers to the number of measurement occasions per day. For ED tasks, the number of stimuli refers to the total set (i.e., the sum of positive, negative, and/or neutral stimuli).

3.3. Emotional Vocabulary

As illustrated in Table 3, the large majority of studies (97.39%, n = 112) have so far assessed ED using predefined sets of emotional labels, whereas a scant yet growing portion of studies has relied on freely generated emotion language (5.22%, n = 6). Given that emotional lexicon varies considerably across languages and cultures, the way individuals conceptualize and express emotions is deeply influenced by their linguistic and cultural context (Mesquita et al., 2017). The current body of literature is heavily skewed toward English-speaking contexts; the majority of studies (n = 73) have been conducted in countries such as the United States, Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, New Zealand, and Singapore. A smaller number of studies have been carried out in other languages, including Dutch (n = 18; Netherlands and Belgium), Chinese (n = 10), German (n = 8; Germany and Austria), Danish (n = 4), Japanese (n = 4), Hebrew (n = 2; Israel), Russian (n = 1; Russia), and Hindi (n = 1; India).

3.3.1. Use of Predefined Emotion Labels in Assessing Emotion Differentiation

We found several differences across studies in the number and type of labels employed, as well as in the rating scales that participants are instructed to use to assess the intensity of their emotional experience. A complete list of emotional labels, categorized by valence and ranked by frequency of use across studies, is presented in Table S4 in the Supplemental Material.

A first source of variability lies in the valence of emotional labels presented to participants:

Consistent with the goal of examining positive and negative ED, most studies have included both positive and negative emotion labels; a second group of studies has used negative-valence labels only, whereas a few studies (Tugade et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021) have focused on positive-valence labels only. Notably, few studies also included a "neutral" label, which was then used in the calculation of both positive and negative ED scores (Hoemann, Barrett, et al., 2021; Hoemann et al., 2023; Hoemann, Khan, et al., 2021; Petagna & Wormwood, 2025).

Second, we observed considerable variability in the number of emotional labels, ranging from a minimum of 3 to a maximum of 39 (M = 12.40, SD = 6.51). Researchers have generally privileged the inclusion of negative emotional labels (M = 8.25, SD = 5.19, range 3-35) over the inclusion of positive emotional labels (M = 6.62, SD = 3.20, range 1-19).

A third difference concerns the nature (i.e., mentalistic vs. bodily; Ip et al., 2024) and level of specificity of emotion words (Brown et al., 2021; Erbas et al., 2016; Kashdan et al., 2010; Lazarus et al., 2022; Matt et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2023; Sheets et al., 2015; Starr et al., 2017; Vandercammen et al., 2014; Walters et al., 2023; Williams-Kerver & Crowther, 2020; Yue et al., 2024). Regarding the nature of emotional labels, most studies have used mentalistic emotion labels (e.g., contented, enraged), whereas a smaller yet significant subset of studies has also administered "bodily" terms (e.g., tired, relaxed, energetic). When using a limited number of labels, researchers have relied mostly on terms reflecting the so-called "basic emotions" (e.g., happy, angry). Other mentalistic labels used in this literature reflect social (e.g., ashamed, embarrassed, guilty, scornful) or cognitively laden emotions (e.g., curious, interested, distracted, capable). Concerning the level of specificity, some researchers have included only highly specific and presumably more "granular" emotion terms (e.g., repentant, blameworthy, and resentful), whereas others have also administered more generic descriptors (e.g., uneasy, dislike, down, and droopy).

Additional heterogeneity comes from the number of emotion categories considered and the number of labels included within each category by each study. Some studies have included multiple labels belonging to different emotion families (e.g., Hill & Updegraff, 2012; Israelashvili et al., 2019; Mehak et al., 2024), whereas other studies have employed a single label per category, thus resulting in limited representativeness of the broader emotional spectrum (e.g., Lv et al., 2024; Walukevich-Dienst et al., 2023; Yang, 2023). Negative emotion categories are more frequently represented, encompassing clusters related to sadness (e.g., depressed, tearful), fear (e.g., anxious, worried), anger (e.g., irritable, enraged), guilt (e.g., guilty, blameworthy), shame (e.g., embarrassed, humiliated), and disgust (e.g., repulsed, scornful). Positive emotion categories most often include happiness (e.g., joyful, content), excitement (e.g., enthusiastic, exhilarated), and calmness (e.g., peaceful, serene).

Notably, the number of labels included in positive and negative emotion categories is often not equal.

Finally, most studies have used Likert-type scales, with the number of scale points varying from a minimum of 4 to a maximum of 11. A smaller subset of studies has employed slider scales, generally ranging from 0-100 or from 1-100 (for an exception see Matyi & Spielberg, 2023).

3.3.2. Use of Natural Language in Assessing Emotion Differentiation

Among studies using natural language approaches, participants have been asked to describe their emotional experience through open-ended narratives (Williams & Uliaszek, 2022) or through freely generated emotion labels (Ottenstein & Lischetzke, 2020; Potthoff et al., 2023; Seah & Coifman, 2024; Wabnegger et al., 2024).

Compared with the use of predefined sets of labels, the natural language approach requires some sort of coding procedures to identify emotion-related words and distinguish them from a more general affective language. Notably, we found that only roughly half of the studies described such procedures, which included the use of text analysis software such as RIOT Scan (Boyd, 2014) and Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count ([LIWC]; Pennebaker et al., 2015), or the use of a preexisting corpus of emotion words (e.g., Johnson-Laird and Oatley, 1989). In this latter case, custom dictionaries were developed by expanding existing emotion corpora and including the emotion terms generated by the participants.

Coding procedures have also been employed to determine the valence and specificity of emotion words. Positive and negative emotion terms have been commonly distinguished via either valence ratings (Potthoff et al., 2023; Wabnegger et al., 2024) or top-down categorization based on inter-rater agreement (Seah & Coifman, 2024). However, half of the studies did not report the criteria used to distinguish positive, negative, and neutral words.

Likewise, although all the studies have made distinctions between specific versus general terms (or between specific, general, and basic emotion terms; Williams & Uliaszek, 2022), in many cases, the criteria used to make such distinctions have not been explicitly reported.

Some exceptions include Williams and Uliaszek (2022), who relied on the corpus by Johnson-Laird and Oatley (1989), and Ottenstein and Lischetzke (2020), who used the Levels of Emotional Awareness Scale (LEAS; Lane et al., 1990). Finally, within this approach, only two studies (out of six) have asked the participants to rate the intensity of each self-generated emotion label (Seah & Coifman, 2024; Wabnegger et al., 2024). Note: The sum of the analytical components (n) may be greater than the total number of studies (N) because some studies included multiple dimensions of operationalization (e.g., some studies administered both positive and negative emotional labels). The sum of the total number of studies employing each computational method (N) exceeds the total number of studies included in the review (i.e., 115 studies) because some studies assessed emotion differentiation scores via both fixed emotion labels and natural language. "Emotion Lexicon Classification" refers to the method used to classify the identified emotion lexicon as specific, basic, or generic.

3.4. Computational Procedures

We can distinguish between two main computational approaches that have been implemented to derive ED indices (Table 4).

The first approach relies on the variability of the intensity ratings provided to a fixed set of emotion labels that have been repeatedly administered over time (either through ESM protocols or the ED task). The second approach derives the ED index from an evaluation of the specificity of the emotion lexicon generated by participants with their own words.

Computation procedures for all ED indices are described in Table 5.

3.4.1. Indices Based on the Variability of Intensity Ratings

When examining variance-based computation methods, we were confronted with a complex puzzle of different measures. Specifically, the procedures employed to compute ED indices were different depending on whether the study intended to capture dispositional, daily, or momentary ED.

Dispositional Emotion Differentiation.

The most widely used approach to measuring dispositional ED involves the computation of intraclass correlation (ICC) coefficients. Another (far less common) method is calculating average inter-item correlation (AIC) coefficients. Finally, a small number of studies have employed even less conventional methods such as principal component analysis (PCA) (Grühn et al., 2013; Mikkelsen et al., 2020), the mean-standard-deviation (MSD) method (Huggins et al. 2023), the average daily variance of emotion ratings (VAR) (Mikhail et al. 2020), and the Multiple Emotion Co-Activation (MECA) index (Ready et al., 2019).

Momentary Emotion Differentiation.

The most widely adopted approach to compute momentary ED indices consists of an adaptation of the dispositional ICC-based method to the level of single measurement occasions (Erbas, Kalokerinos, et al., 2022; Seah & Coifman, 2024; Sels et al., 2024; Springstein et al., 2023) via the formula proposed by Erbas et al. (2022). Although few studies have so far examined momentary ED, alternative approaches have been proposed to account for the variability in ED patterns over time, such as the Latent Markov Factor Analysis (LMFA) (Schmitt et al., 2024) and the variance components procedure (PROC VARCOMP) (Racine et al., 2024).

Daily Emotion Differentiation.

The PROC VARCOMP approach has also been used to compute daily ED (Bicaker et al., 2022), averaging momentary indices across multiple assessments within the same day. In contrast, Lischetzke et al. (2021) have calculated daily ED by adapting the formula proposed by Erbas et al. (2022)to the daily level. Other studies (Erbas et al., 2018; Hoemann, Barrett, et al., 2021; O'Toole et al., 2021) have computed daily ICC-based ED relying on observations confined to a single day.

3.4.2. Indices Based on the Variability of Intensity Ratings: Computational Choices

Besides the significant variability in the computation methods of ED indices we described above, an additional shortcoming concerns the different ways in which researchers have handled some methodological choices related to the computation itself. The first issue concerns negative ICCs.

Although these coefficients are theoretically constrained between 0 and 1, negative values can emerge due to measurement error (Shrout & Fleiss, 1979). Negative ICCs are common in ED research (for exceptions, see Kalokerinos et al., 2019; Pugach et al., 2023), yet we could not find any information about how they were handled in about half of the studies included in the review. Among the remaining studies, some have excluded negative ICCs from further analysis (e.g., Liao et al., 2025; Oh & Tong, 2020; Seah, Sidney, et al., 2022) while others have recorded them as zero (e.g., Bonar et al., 2023; Sels et al., 2024; Thompson, Liu, et al., 2021).

A related issue concerns the choice of ICC method. Although ICCs can be estimated on the basis of either absolute agreement (e.g., Eckland et al., 2021; Emery et al., 2014; Mankus et al., 2016) or consistency (e.g., Dawel et al., 2023; Seah, Almahmoud, et al., 2022; Van Der Gucht et al., 2019), approximately one-third of the studies did not report any information regarding the type of method employed (e.g., Decker et al., 2008; Tong & Keng, 2017; Wang et al., 2024; Yang, 2022). It has been argued that only correlations (i.e., consistency method) are theoretically meaningful for ED, yet empirical evidence suggests that consistency and agreement estimates are highly correlated (r = .95-.99, p < .001; Erbas et al., 2014).

Another common issue, which encompasses all the computational methods, concerns the instances in which emotion ratings exhibit no variability. Such within-person zero-variability cases may stem from both high levels of ED (e.g., a high-ED individual may not find their emotional state adequately represented by any of the provided emotional labels) or low levels of ED (e.g., low-ED individuals may rate in the same way all emotions). Although zero-variability cases are not rare in practice, information about their prevalence and the methods used to handle them is largely absent from most studies. Among the few studies reporting it, some researchers using ICC-based indices opted to exclude these cases from the analysis (Berman et al., 2022; Kashdan & Farmer, 2014; Matt et al., 2024) due to their non-interpretability. Other researchers using PROC VARCOMP-based indices have either coded these ICCs as zero/one or excluded them from the analyses, depending on the specific characterization of the zero-variability cases (e.g., excluding cases where both positive and negative items are all rated as "very slightly or not at all", while imputing scores as 1 when all items of only one valence were rated as "very slightly or not at all") (Bicaker et al., 2022; Racine et al., 2024).

Of note, the issue concerning zero-variability cases is particularly relevant when computing state-level ED indices via either the PROC VARCOMP procedure or the formula proposed by Erbas et al. (2022). Both methods depend on variance terms in the denominator, making the index noncomputable when the variance is zero. For PROC VARCOMP, this occurs when items exhibit no variability both within and across observations, whereas for the Erbas et al. (2022) formula, the problem arises when each item shows no variability across observations. While the two studies employing the PROC VARCOMP procedure have either coded such zero-variability instances as zero/one or excluded them from the analyses (Bicaker et al., 2022; Racine et al., 2024), only one study (Matt et al., 2024) adopting the Erbas et al. (2022) formula provided information about how they handled such cases (i.e., exclusion).

A last methodological issue inherent to the Erbas et al. (2022) formula involves those instances in which the numerator equals zero. Critically, a zero numerator may arise either when at a certain time point every emotion rating equals the person's mean for that emotion (i.e., each person-mean-centered value is exactly 0), or when the person-mean centered ratings for each emotion at a certain time point, once averaged, canceled out to (approximately) zero, even though there is variability in the ratings.

These two scenarios reflect distinct underlying interpretations of ED; however, none of the studies included in the review explicitly reported how such cases were treated.

Finally, an additional issue concerns the choice of how ED is calculated within specific ED conceptualizations. Concerning global ED, most studies have computed separate ICC-based indices (Edwards & Wupperman, 2017; Hoemann, Khan, et al., 2021; Huggins et al., 2019; Ikeda, 2023; Liu et al., 2020) or AIC-based indices (O'Toole et al., 2014) for positive and negative emotions and then averaged the two indices to derive a measure of dispositional global ED; by contrast, others have calculated global ICC-based (Grühn et al., 2013; Lukic et al., 2023), AIC-based (Kimhy et al., 2014) or PCA-based (Grühn et al., 2013) indices across positive and negative emotion labels. For withincategory ED, computation included both category-specific indices (e.g., differentiation among sadness-related emotions) and a single score obtained by averaging those category-specific indices across all assessed categories (Erbas et al., 2019; Willroth et al., 2020; for an exception, see Plonsker et al., 2017). Lastly, as described above, for daily ICC-based ED both the dispositional and the momentary formulas have been adjusted.

3.4.3. Indices Based on the Specificity of the Emotional Lexicon

Within the natural language approach, Ottenstein and Lischetzke (2020) have introduced a Specificity Index (SI) of ED that is calculated by coding freely generated emotion words as either specific (e.g., anxious, irritated, sad) or general (e.g., bad, negative, unpleasant). The SI is then computed as the proportion of specific adjectives out of the total number of emotion adjectives used.

The SI has been calculated at the state level (Seah & Coifman, 2024) and at the dispositional level by aggregating all momentary or daily entries across time (Ottenstein & Lischetzke, 2020; Potthoff et al., 2023; Williams & Uliaszek, 2022).

A revised version of the SI has been recently proposed by Williams and Uliaszek (2022) with the introduction of the nuance score (NS). To derive this index, emotion words are first coded as either general (coded as 1), basic (coded as 2), or specific (coded as 3); then, the ratings of all adjectives are summed and divided by the total number of terms used. Like the SI, the NS has been originally developed to quantify ED at the dispositional level but is also suitable for state-level assessments.

Finally, a third, more recent version of the SI (Wabnegger et al., 2024) consists of a performance-based ED score that is calculated based on interrater agreement, with scores averaged across reports to produce an overall index. The sum of the total number of studies employing each computational method (N) exceeds the total number of studies included in the review (i.e., 115 studies) because some studies computed emotion differentiation scores via multiple methods (e.g., some studies have computed both ICC-based and AIC-based emotion differentiation indices). "ICC(A, k)" indicates Absolute Agreement-Method for intraclass correlation; "ICC(C, k)" indicates Consistency-Method for intraclass correlation. "Zero-variance" indicates handling of measurement occasions where all emotion labels were rated identically. "Other Methods" includes LMFA-based index (momentary emotion differentiation), MECA index, MSD-based index, sum of the correspondence ratings of items, and average of daily variances (dispositional emotion differentiation). For global emotion differentiation, across index computation procedures, some studies derived separate valence-specific indices and subsequently combined them (e.g., by summing or averaging), whereas others computed indices using all emotion ratings irrespective of valence. For daily emotion differentiation, across computational approaches, some studies adapted dispositional methods to the daily level, whereas others implemented daily adaptations of momentary index computation procedures.

3.4.4. Convergent Validity among Different Computational Procedures

Given the considerable variety of computational methods, some studies included in this review have compared multiple computational approaches to examine convergence across indices.

The results, however, are mixed. For instance, no significant correlations have been found between the ICC-based index on the one side and the PCA-based index (Grühn et al., 2013) or the VAR-based index on the other (Mikhail et al., 2020). Likewise, the VAR-and AIC-based indices were also found to be unrelated (Mikhail et al., 2020). Conversely, the ICC-based and AIC-based indices appeared to be highly correlated (Mikhail et al., 2020).

Other studies have also examined the associations between ED indices derived from different assessment approaches (i.e., fixed sets of emotion labels vs. spontaneous use of emotional vocabulary). The correlations between the ICC-based index and the SI or the NS were nonsignificant or inconsistent for both positive and negative emotions (Ottenstein & Lischetzke, 2020; Seah & Coifman, 2024; Williams & Uliaszek, 2022). By contrast, the SI and NS were found to be moderately correlated (Williams & Uliaszek, 2022).

Finally, few studies have compared within-category, between-category, and integral ICCbased indices. The integral and between-category indices were highly correlated, whereas their correlation with the aggregated, within-category index was lower (Erbas et al., 2019). When examining separate within-category indices referring to different emotion categories, weak intercorrelations were found, suggesting that the ability to differentiate within an emotion category (e.g., anger) should not be generalized to other categories (e.g., fear). Similar findings have been reported by Willroth et al. (2020). ICC-based Intraclass correlation (ICC) followed by Fisher's r-to-z transformation and reverse-coded. 3.5. Emotion Differentiation Correlates

When examining the potential correlates of ED, we found that these variables can be grouped into two main areas. First, several studies (38.26%, n = 44) have examined the relationship between ED and constructs such as emotion regulation, alexithymia, emotional intensity, emotional clarity, and dialecticism. Emotion regulation emerges as the most common correlate -unsurprisingly, as ED has been speculated to function as a form of regulation (Kashdan et al., 2015). Despite this thematic overlap, these studies revealed substantial methodological heterogeneity. Approximately one-third of the studies assessed ED via the ED task, while merely all the studies employed a fixed set of emotion labels (for an exception, see Seah & Coifman, 2024). ED conceptualizations also varied: Most studies investigated dispositional ED, with only few studies investigating momentary (Schmitt et al., 2024; Seah & Coifman, 2024; Sels et al., 2024; Springstein et al., 2023) and daily ED (Hoemann, Barrett, et al., 2021; O'Toole et al., 2021). Notably, negative ED was examined nearly twice as often as positive ED. Furthermore, about half of these studies were conducted with English-speaking participants and student samples.

The second area concerns psychological well-being and mental health (27.83%, n = 32). Within this area, ED has been associated with both adaptive (e.g., life satisfaction, subjective well-being) and maladaptive (e.g., stress, depressive and anxiety symptoms) outcomes. Some studies have directly compared ED in clinical and nonclinical populations, including individuals suffering from schizophrenia (Kimhy et al., 2014b), posttraumatic stress (Pugach et al., 2023) and depression (Springstein et al., 2023). Measurement approaches emerged as relatively balanced across ecological methods (i.e., EMA, diary) and ED tasks. Despite some studies assessed ED using natural language reports (Ottenstein & Lischetzke, 2020), most studies employed fixed emotion labels. Few studies assessed momentary ED (Erbas, Kalokerinos, et al., 2022), while all other studies examined ED at the dispositional level. Again, approximately half were conducted with English-speaking participants and student samples.

Other studies have investigated the association between ED and maladaptive behaviors (13.8%, n = 12), such as verbal or physical aggression; substance (alcohol, tobacco, or cannabis) use and craving; and impulsivity. All these studies assessed dispositional ED using the ICC-based method to compute the index (for an exception examining momentary ED using the PROC VARCOMP, see Racine et al., 2024). All but one (Edwards & Wupperman, 2017) employed ecological designs. These studies were all conducted with English-speaking participants and approximately three-quarters were based on student samples.

Finally, a smaller set of studies have examined ED in relation to cognitive processes (6.09%, n = 7; e.g., moral judgment), eating behavior (4.35%, n = 5; e.g., loss of control over eating), social behavior (4.35%, n = 5; e.g., helping behavior), mindfulness (3.48%, n = 4), personality traits (2.61%, n = 3; e.g., neuroticism), romantic relationships (1.74%, n = 2; e.g., relationship quality), and adaptive behavior (0.87%, n = 1; i.e., medication adherence). Across all these topics, methodological heterogeneity remains a defining feature. Studies differed in ED conceptualization, measurement approach and study designs, the statistical method to index computation, and the type of sample included.

4. Discussion

The present systematic review highlights substantial heterogeneity in how ED is conceptualized and assessed both within and across thematic domains. In the following sections, we first discuss the main open questions arising from the different conceptual dimensions of ED. We then move to ED operationalization, examining the methodological concerns associated with current ED assessment practices and their implications for the validity, interpretation, and comparability of findings across studies. Building on these considerations, we discuss the need to align measurement practices more closely with the theoretical meaning of ED and consider what is ultimately captured by an ED measure. We conclude by proposing recommendations for transparent measurement reporting and outlining a research agenda aimed at strengthening ED measurement.

4.1. Conceptual Dimensions of Emotion Differentiation: Open Questions

Within the literature on emotion differentiation, methodological developments and theoretical refinement have often progressed in parallel, gradually expanding the conceptual boundaries of ED.

Our review corroborates that ED is far from a monolithic construct, encompassing distinctions of temporal framing, representational scope of emotion categories, and valence. These distinctions represent an important refinement of how ED has been defined and studied. At the same time, it is unclear how the different ED conceptualizations relate to one another and whether they show similar or distinct patterns of association with psychological functioning.

Temporal framing provides one example of this unresolved issue. Early research implicitly treated ED as a relatively stable dispositional characteristic, and only recently has it begun to be investigated at the daily or momentary level. First, such fine-grained temporal resolutions raise questions about what drives short-term fluctuations in ED. Some studies have begun to address this issue by extracting contextual variables to account for situational influences (Hoemann et al., 2023), suggesting that differentiation ability may vary across contexts and life periods (Erbas et al., 2018; Schmitt et al., 2024; Springstein et al., 2023).

Second, the relationship between dispositional and state-level ED also needs clarification: Whether dispositional and state-level ED reflect distinct yet complementary processes, and whether they influence each other over time, remains an open question. For instance, individuals high in dispositional ED might show momentary drops under overwhelming events, whereas those low in dispositional ED might show momentary increases in particular situations. Additionally, dispositional ED may shape momentary fluctuations, and, in turn, state-level ED may contribute to the development of more enduring emotion differentiation abilities.

Finally, because most research has so far focused on dispositional ED, it remains unclear whether the functional role attributed to ED at the dispositional level extends to daily and momentary levels.

Fluctuations in differentiation may reflect the same underlying processes expressed at different temporal scales or may arise from partly distinct mechanisms with different adaptive or maladaptive implications.

A similar issue arises from the distinction between integral and category-specific ED.

Preliminary evidence suggests that differentiating between distinct emotion categories is typically easier than differentiating within a given category, and that this ability may vary by emotion family (Erbas et al., 2019; Willroth et al., 2020). This distinction offers a promising avenue for examining whether the functional significance of ED varies across emotion categories. The ability to differentiate among emotions within one category (e.g., anger) may be associated with an aspect of psychological functioning (e.g., stress, expressive suppression), whereas the ability to differentiate among emotions within another category (e.g., sadness) may be related to a different outcome (e.g., depressive symptoms, rumination).

Valence represents a third dimension along which the literature remains uneven. Although positive and negative ED are commonly distinguished, negative ED has received substantially greater empirical attention than positive or global ED. This imbalance may partly reflect differences in the characteristics of positive and negative emotional experiences. Positive emotions may be more fluid, less categorically bounded, and more likely to involve blended labeling (Vlasenko et al., 2021), potentially making their differentiation more difficult to operationalize. Nevertheless, the relative scarcity of research on positive ED leaves open the question of whether positive and negative ED shows comparable associations with psychological functioning or instead exhibit partly distinct patterns. Establishing whether the different valence-specific forms of ED are functionally equivalent is therefore a relevant unresolved issue.

Importantly, these three conceptual dimensions should be conceived as interrelated rather than independent. For example, between-and within-category ED may help explain context-dependent fluctuations in differentiation, as the ability to distinguish among emotional states may vary depending on the interplay between emotion category and situational context. Likewise, because within-category ED requires more fine-grained discrimination within a narrower emotional domain, greater differentiation may not necessarily carry the same implications across valence. For instance, a more fine-grained focus on positive emotional experiences may have adaptive implications, whereas extensive differentiation among negative emotions may be associated with different, and potentially less adaptive, outcomes. Identifying and accounting for these sources of variability in the individuals' capacity to precisely distinguish between emotional states represents a promising avenue for refining our understanding of ED and its functional significance.

4.2. Main Concerns Associated with Current Operationalizations

Inconsistencies in assessment, together with important gaps in reporting practices, are evident within each of the three methodological dimensions identified in our review (i.e., measurement approach, emotional vocabulary, and computation procedures) and raise distinct concerns for validity, reliability, replicability, generalizability, and cross-study comparability of ED measures. In the following sections, we therefore consider these concerns separately for each methodological dimension, with the corresponding implications summarized in Table 6. Importantly, although we examine methodological concerns separately within each dimension, it is worth noting that methodological choices across these dimensions can be combined in different ways, potentially introducing multiple and overlapping layers of methodological concerns within a single operationalization. Most studies used affective pictures (N = 19); others used autobiographical recall (N = 6), scenarios (N = 5), affective clips (N = 4), pictures and news headlines (N = 2), decision-making trials (N = 1), or tasks involving naming target persons (N = 1).

2. Valence of stimuli Comparability

Most studies used both positive and negative stimuli (N = 18) or negative only (N = 14); few used positive only (N = 2) or stimuli for which a valence distinction was not applicable (N = 4).

3. Number of stimuli Generalizability, reliability

The number of stimuli ranged from 6-50 when both positive and negative stimuli were included and from 10-34 for single-valence studies; most administered 6-10 stimuli (N = 11) or 16-20 stimuli (N = 13).

4. Temporal frame of reference

Comparability, construct validity, generalizability Studies relying on scenarios and autobiographical information studies (N = 12) relied on retrospective frame of reference, while the remainder captured immediate emotional experience (N = 26).

5. Setting Comparability, generalizability, reliability, replicability

Studies were mostly conducted in laboratory settings (N = 29), the remainder online.

Content validity, comparability, generalizability

Negative labels ranged from 3-35 (N = 109); positive labels from 1-19 (N = 68); a "neutral" label was rarely included (N = 4). Mentalistic terms were markedly overrepresented relative to bodily terms, though the latter also administered (negative: N = 43; positive: N = 50).

Studies used specific terms and some also included generic descriptors (negative: N = 49; positive: N = 4). The most recurring emotional categories were sadness (e.g., depressed, tearful; N = 95), anger (e.g., irritable, enraged; N = 94), guilt (e.g., guilty, blameworthy; N = 58), shame (e.g., embarrassed, humiliated; N = 58), fear (e.g., anxious, worried; N = 55), disgust (e.g., repulsed, scornful; N = 42), happiness (e.g., joyful, content; N = 68), calmness (e.g., peaceful, serene; N = 61), and excitement (e.g., enthusiastic, exhilarated; N = 44).

Lexicons drew on pre-existing resources (N = 4) or unspecified procedures (N = 2). All studies assessed negative vocabulary; only a minority also included positive vocabulary (N = 2).

Negative ICC Reliability, construct validity, criterion validity, replicability Among ICC-based studies (N = 99), most did not report how negative ICCs were handled (N = 58); others excluded them (N = 14) or coded them as missing (N = 18) or zero (N = 9).

Computed via consistency (N = 42) or agreement (N = 37); a substantial share did not specify the method (N = 32).

Only a few studies (N = 10) explicitly reported zerovariance handling: excluded (N = 5), treated as missing (N = 1), or coded as missing or assigned a value of 0/1 (N = 2). Two studies reported that no zero-variance cases occurred.

4. ED computation within specific conceptual dimensions

Construct validity, reliability, comparability Global ED was computed as a single index across labels (ICC-based N = 6; AIC-based N = 1), as a sum of item ratings (N = 1), or by averaging separate negative/positive indices (ICC-based N = 3; PCA-based N = 1). Within-category ED was computed as categoryspecific indices (N = 3) or as a single score averaging those indices across categories (N = 1). Daily ED was computed by averaging momentary PCA-based scores (N =1) and adapting the momentary (N = 1) or dispositional (N = 3) ICC-based formula at the daily level.

5. Sensitivity to within-person variability

Comparability, construct validity, generalizability, reliability, replicability Variance-based indices (N = 112) are highly sensitive to within-person variability regardless of computational method. This holds particularly true for momentary ICCbased indices (N = 8) which can involve both zeronumerator or zero-denominator cases.

Relying on Natural Language (N = 6) 1. Procedures to treat linguistic information (coding, weighting, aggregating)

Construct validity, comparability, generalizability

Emotion words were classified either dichotomously as general vs. specific (N = 4) or along three levels of specificity, i.e., general, basic, or specific (N = 1); one study instead derived the coding from the degree of agreement among raters. Some studies assigned equal weight to all specific words (N = 4), one assigned increasing weights to each level of specificity (1, 2, or 3 points), and one weighted each report by inter-rater agreement. Scores were computed as the proportion of specific adjectives out of all emotion adjectives used (N = 4), as the sum of the points divided by the total number of terms (N = 1), or as the average of agreement-based scores across reports (N = 1).

2. Dependence on the total number of emotion words Reliability, construct validity

All studies (N = 6) used indices inherently dependent on the total number of emotion words produced.

4.2.1. Methodological Concerns Related to Measurement Approaches

Our analyses revealed high variability in the duration of data collection and in the sampling rate of emotional episodes, both in ESM and ED task studies. Such variability raises questions about a "reasonable" minimum-maximum number of measurement occasions that is needed to capture meaningful emotional experiences. Indeed, protocols heterogeneity not only raises concerns about comparability and the generalizability of findings but also calls into question the reliability of the emotional episodes sampled: If measurement occasions are too frequent, participant burden may bias responses; if too sparse, they may fail to fully capture the complexity of emotional processes.

A second critical issue concerns differences in the temporal frame of reference. While some methodological approaches (e.g., EMA, ED tasks involving an immediate response to some sort of emotional stimuli) are meant to measure current emotional experience, other approaches (e.g., diary methods, the DRM, ED tasks based on autobiographic recall) require participants to remember and reconstruct past events. This variability also extends to studies assessing ED through open-ended descriptions, where participants may be asked to report on either present or past emotional events.

Although retrospective evaluations may provide more nuanced emotional descriptions due to the cognitive processing of experiences (Kashdan et al., 2015; Thompson, Springstein, et al., 2021), such methods cast doubt on what the researcher is actually measuring, whether meta-reflective processes related to emotional understanding or ED. Critically, given the near-equal use of immediate and retrospective methods, treating them as interchangeable remains questionable, with potential implications for validity, cross-study comparability, and generalizability of findings.

We also found inconsistencies in ED task studies, with large differences in the number of trials, the instructions, and the setting of data collection. ED tasks were originally introduced to address a key limitation of ESM: The natural variability in the number and type of emotional episodes a participant may encounter over time (Erbas et al., 2014). By using standardized stimuli, researchers have attempted to enhance control and comparability across individuals. However, individual differences in the personal relevance and emotional impact of standardized stimuli remain largely unexplored, and differences in task characteristics may itself drive variability in ED estimates independent of true differentiation ability. These issues ultimately raise concerns regarding validity, reliability and cross-study comparability.

Finally, the last major point of debate is whether ecological and nonecological methods yield convergent results (Thompson, Springstein, et al., 2021). Erbas et al. (2014) reported that ED indices derived from both EMA and ED tasks produced similar results, suggesting that the two methods may capture overlapping constructs. In contrast, Ventura-Bort et al. (2021) reported divergent results when ED scores from an ED task and the DRM were compared. Likewise, Erbas et al. (2019) observed that ED indices obtained via ESM and ED tasks were only weakly correlated, further challenging the assumption that these approaches tap into the same underlying construct. Together, these findings challenge the assumption that ecological and non-ecological approaches tap into the same underlying construct, casting doubts about the validity of ED as currently assessed.

4.2.2. Methodological Concerns Related to Emotion Vocabulary

To date, ED has been mostly assessed using fixed sets of emotional labels. Although this approach offers standardization across participants within the same study, some shortcomings deserve careful consideration. First and foremost, the lack of shared criteria for label selection (in terms of number and type of labels) may lead to inconsistent measurement of ED and low cross-study comparability. The lexical context in which emotion labels are presented plays a crucial role, as the presence or absence of semantically similar terms in a list can influence both the granularity of differentiation and the interpretation of the meaning of a given emotion label. Thus, participants' ability to capture subtle emotional distinctions may be biased when they are presented with lists of labels in which emotional categories are represented by few (or a single) terms, or in which the labels differ in their level of specificity (general vs. specific) or affective nature (mentalistic vs. bodily).

Beyond these methodological considerations, the lack of shared criteria in the use of predefined emotion labels also raises important concerns regarding content validity. When providing them with predefined labels, researchers assume that participants are familiar with those labels and the terms adequately capture their experience (Ip et al., 2024; Li et al., 2020). However, this assumption may not hold true across individuals and contexts, thus the use of a fixed-label approach may lead to biased knowledge of people's actual ED skills (Ottenstein & Lischetzke, 2020). Assessing the subjectivity of another's experience, which is meaningful only as appraised by the perceiver themselves, is a delicate endeavor that risks falling into fallacy if not approached with appropriate caution. This epistemological caveat speaks directly to the broad range of inter-and intra-individual variability in emotional instances, rooted in the individual's culture, languages, and experiential background (Barrett, 2009; Mesquita et al., 2017). Individuals may also differ in the extent to which they experience emotions as bodily sensations or mental events (Ip et al., 2024). These considerations call for a more reflexive use of fixed-label approaches as necessarily constrained approximations of individuals' emotional processes (Bringmann et al., 2026; Hoemann, Warfel, et al., 2025; Stadel et al., 2025).

Although assessment methods based on natural language have been far less frequently employed in ED research, they offer a promising alternative to fixed-label approaches, since they have the potential to capture more authentic and contextually grounded verbal expressions. Like the fixed-label approach, however, we identified some shortcomings that must be carefully addressed, as they may hinder construct validity and cross-study comparability. A key issue concerns the coding procedures that researchers have used to identify "emotion" terms and to classify such terms as "specific", "basic", or "general" for ED scoring and as either positive or negative (in this latter case, for some words the distinction may not be straightforward; e.g., surprised, impressed, impatient).

Because emotion concepts cannot be fully reduced to individual words (Hoemann, 2024; Hoemann, Lee, et al., 2025), and because they are deeply shaped by individuals' personal background (Barrett, 2009; Barrett et al., 2007) and cultural context (Mesquita et al., 2017), these classifications inevitably entail some form of arbitrary interpretation. Inter-rater agreement offers one consistency check, yet the coding process is tendentious and may be influenced by judges' own conceptual backgrounds, theoretical expertise and emotional fluency. Standardized tools, meanwhile, reflect the theoretical assumptions of their creators, rarely capture the context in which emotion words are used, and are not equally available for all languages and cultures. All these alternatives are therefore not entirely free from biases and cannot fully account for situated meaning or conceptual nuance. Of note, we remark that a major shortcoming of existing studies is that, in many cases, detailed information about the coding procedures we described above is omitted.

A further open issue concerns information that can be extracted from natural language beyond individual emotion words. This includes, first, how to deal with paraphrased or metaphorical language (e.g., "I missed the ground beneath my feet"), which may reflect either partially articulated or highly complex emotions not mapping onto conventional labels. As broader expressions of abstract concepts, such expressions inherently introduce ambiguity with respect to the interpretation of ED levels.

Nevertheless, they often convey blended or complex emotional experiences that, despite being difficult to categorize, are still informative (Fetterman et al., 2022). A related issue concerns the role of modifiers (e.g., adverbs, adjectives): While indicating emotional intensity, they can also reflect an individual's ED levels. For example, if the term "furious" suggests a high intensity emotional experience (e.g., compared with "angry"), the expression "extremely furious" could denote added intensity or a more fine-grained experience. Therefore, more work is needed to discuss the role of modifiers and how to potentially treat them (Sintsova et al., 2017; Yu & Lai, 2014).

4.2.3. Methodological Concerns Related to Indices Computation

So far, research has used a plethora of computational indices to quantify ED. Across literature estimating ED from the variability of intensity ratings, key computational choices were often implemented inconsistently and, in many cases, not reported at all. First, the lack of standardized criteria for computational decisions may contribute to differences in ED scores that are attributable to methodological choices rather than to differences in the underlying construct. This includes, for instance, whether retaining, excluding or re-coding negative ICCs and zero-variability cases, how to handle zero values in the numerator of the Erbas et al. (2022) formula, which ICC specification (i.e., consistency vs. agreement) should be adopted, and how to handle ED computation within specific conceptual dimensions (e.g., when assessing global ED, whether deriving a single index by averaging separate positive-and negative-valence indices or by estimating the index directly across all emotion categories). This computational heterogeneity therefore should be explicitly considered when comparing findings across studies. A further consideration is that these indices are highly sensitive to within-person variability. Consequently, naturally occurring fluctuations in individuals' affective experiences across time or contexts may be translated into statistical artifacts rather than genuine differences in ED, raising important concerns about the validity, reliability, and between-person comparability of existing ED estimates.

By contrast, although computational approaches based on the specificity of natural language avoid imposing predefined emotion labels in favor of the variety and richness of emotional responses, they introduce methodological constraints that have received limited attention. First, although these indices share the general aim of capturing the specificity of emotion-related language, they differ in how linguistic information is coded, weighted, and aggregated, meaning that the resulting scores are not necessarily directly comparable. Another major issue concerns the dependence of these indices on the total emotion word count. Natural language indices are expressed as proportions (e.g., the ratio of unique specific to total emotion words), meaning that identical specificity scores may derive from substantially different emotional vocabularies. On the one hand, individuals with the same lexical specificity score may differ markedly in the variety of specific emotion words they use. On the other hand, a rich and diverse emotional vocabulary should not be equated with a differentiated emotional experience, since a larger vocabulary does not necessarily imply greater granularity (DeLap et al., 2024). Current lexical-specificity indices may therefore conflate richness, diversity, and specificity, despite these representing conceptually distinct characteristics of emotional language.

A final consideration concerns the extent to which existing indices can be regarded as equivalent measures of ED. Available evidence suggests that different indices may show only limited convergence, raising questions about the extent to which they capture a common underlying construct.

Thus, computational procedures and the choices underlying them should not be viewed as merely technical aspects of ED measurement: Rather, the use of different computational methods to operationalize ostensibly the same conceptualization of ED may yield substantially different estimates, potentially affecting their validity, reliability, generalizability, and cross-study comparability.

4.3. Bridging Theory and Measurement

Although there is broad agreement that ED refers to an individual's ability to create nuanced instances of emotion, closer examination reveals a degree of theoretical complexity regarding what such differentiation entails in practice. Low ED has been described either as the interchangeable use of multiple discrete emotion labels to communicate an undifferentiated affective experience or as the reliance on broad, generic affective terms; in contrast, high ED has been characterized as the contextsensitive use of multiple discrete emotion labels to capture different facets of an emotional episode, the accurate use of a single discrete emotion concept when it adequately represents the experience, or, more generally, the use of precise and specific emotion concepts to communicate emotional states (Barrett, 2004 (Barrett, , 2006a (Barrett, , 2006b;; Barrett et al., 2001; Tugade et al., 2004). Following these prominent notions, the same linguistic pattern may not necessarily indicate the same level of ED, and different linguistic patterns may not necessarily indicate different levels of ED. For instance, two individuals may both use multiple discrete emotion terms when describing their experiences yet differ markedly in ED: One may use these terms interchangeably to communicate an undifferentiated experience, whereas the other may use them with high specificity to distinguish different facets of the same emotional event. Conversely, low ED might reflect either failure to distinguish among discrete emotion words or reliance on broad, undifferentiated terms. This theoretical complexity has necessarily relevant implications for ED measurement. This issue is further complicated by the fact that ED is conceived as an ability. Ideally, an ED score (i.e., observed variable) should reflect whether an individual is high or low in ED ability (i.e., levels in the latent construct). However, this seemingly straightforward premise conceals a challenging conundrum: Theorizing ED as an ability implies the use of "objective", performance-based measures (Kashdan et al., 2015), applied to inherently subjective experiences. This makes it necessary to determine which observable features of those experiences can serve as evidence of the ability to differentiate emotions.

Addressing this issue is central to the validity of any ED measure, and it can be considered at two related levels: First, what information is collected as the basis for inferring ED; and second, how that information is interpreted and translated into an ED score. As a shared symbolic artifact that renders emotional experience communicable (Barrett, 2006a; Hoemann, 2024), language provides the primary tangible footprint through which ED can be inferred. Accordingly, ED assessment necessarily involves decisions about which linguistic material is collected and the context in which it is collected.

More fundamentally, it concerns the relevant unit of analysis and the degree of lexical freedom that should be allowed during assessment, as well as which properties of language should be considered diagnostic of differentiation. Equally important, however, is how the resulting linguistic information is interpreted. This cannot be reduced simply to how much variation or specificity is observed, but what such patterns are assumed to signify about the underlying ability to differentiate emotions. In other words, patterns of language use should be interpreted in light of assumptions about which properties of emotional labeling are indicative of the underlying ability.

To date, variance-based indices typically interpret high covariation among ratings of a fixed set of distinct emotion terms as evidence of low ED. However, this assumption may be inaccurate under certain conditions: Repeated reports of the same emotion may also reflect stable contextual circumstances (e.g., recurrent anger from repeated conflicts); similarly, co-occurring emotions may stem not only from difficulty distinguishing among one's emotional states, but also from different facets of the same event (e.g., after betrayal one might feel sad due to the end of the relationship, angry for misplaced trust, and indignant at the moral violation) or from the inadequacy of any single label to capture a nuanced experience (e.g., complex or culturally nuanced emotions that lack a direct linguistic equivalent in the individual's native language); lastly, zero-ratings across all emotion labels may reflect either difficulty differentiating emotions or inaccurate available terms. Thus, patterns interpreted statistically as evidence of low ED may sometimes reflect contextual stability, the complexity of emotional experiences, or limitations in available emotion terms rather than reduced differentiation per se. Natural language-based approaches sidestep some of these limitations yet may be less sensitive to forms of low ED characterized by the interchangeable use of multiple specific emotion terms despite poorly differentiated emotional experience.

Taken together, existing methods may provide complementary information on the construct, with the limitations of one approach partly compensated by the strengths of the other. More broadly, >Recommendations and Research Agenda

4.4.1. Reporting Requirements in the Assessment of Emotion Differentiation

We observed that key methodological steps are often unreported across studies, making it difficult to assess the robustness of ED scores and hindering the replicability of findings. These gaps highlight the need for more transparent reporting, aligning with open science principles to enhance reproducibility and cumulative knowledge in the field. Here we propose a set of recommendations for transparency in measurement. Figure 2 summarizes measurement options and reporting requirements (see also Table S5 in the Supplemental Material), organized around the main stages of ED assessment: Conceptualization, measurement approach, emotion vocabulary, and index computation.

First, researchers should justify their conceptualization of ED in line with study's objectives before selecting measurement practices. This includes specifying whether ED is treated as a dispositional or state-level (daily/momentary) construct, whether its representational scope is across, between or within emotion categories, and whether valence focus is positive, negative, or global ED.

These distinctions are not merely methodological choices but reflect different assumptions about ED and should therefore be motivated by a clear theoretical rationale.

Second, researchers should provide more comprehensive descriptions of measurement approaches, being aware that different designs may capture distinct aspects of the construct. Studies relying on natural language approaches should report descriptive information on the amount of emotional (both specific and general) and non-emotional language produced, on average, by each participant and across the sample, as these values underlie the calculation of the reported indices.

Such transparency is worthwhile to provide sufficient detail to allow replication, given that different computational choices may yield different interpretations of the same data.

4.4.2. Evaluating and Refining the Assessment of Emotion Differentiation: Future Directions

As discussed above, the marked heterogeneity in ED measurement may partially stem from both the complexity surrounding the theoretical definition of the construct and the progressive diversification of its conceptualization. Future research should aim to evaluate the reliability and comparability of different assessment procedures while also fostering stronger integration between theoretical definitions and measurement strategies.

First, meta-analytic work on ED measurement is needed to evaluate the construct's robustness across methodological choices, potentially aided by open datasets such as the EMOTE database (Kalokerinos et al., 2026).

Such work could test whether ecological and non-ecological approaches yield interchangeable estimates, whether within-approach variations (e.g., for EMA studies: Assessment duration, number and frequency of daily prompts, compliance criteria) meaningfully affect results, and what minimum assessment number and reports distribution yields reliable estimates. It could also be tested whether the number and characteristics of emotion labels influence ED scores, and whether different natural language coding procedures yield systematically different estimates. Finally, given the limited convergence among indices, future meta-analyses should formally test whether different computation procedures capture the same latent construct or distinct dimensions. This line of inquiry would provide valuable evidence to formulate methodological guidelines for future research.

Second, evaluating and refining methodological procedures requires attention to the theoretical meaning of ED. As a complex and multifaceted construct, ED may be translated into observable indicators in different ways, creating ambiguity in its operationalization. Greater consensus is therefore needed regarding which features of individuals' emotional reports can be considered evidence of the ability to differentiate emotions and, importantly, whether and how these features correspond to the theoretical definition of ED. Collaborative efforts -including working groups, symposia, and round-table discussions -may help advance such consensus. In parallel, the development of new operationalizations should be theory-informed while remaining empirically grounded. Without an iterative dialogue between theory and empirical investigation, new measures risk becoming methodological artifacts that capture properties of the measurement procedure rather than meaningful variation in the underlying construct. One promising direction is to investigate the processes underlying participants' responses during ED assessment, with the aim of understanding how individuals generate and interpret emotion reports and, ultimately, grounding measurement more firmly in the processes underlying the latent construct (Bringmann et al., 2026; Kandala et al., 2025).

Emotion vocabulary is another critical issue: Language alone does not guarantee shared meaning, as emotional concepts are deeply shaped by individuals' personal background (Barrett, 2009; Barrett et al., 2007) and cultural context (Mesquita et al., 2017). Differences in lexical availability across languages and cultures may limit validity and comparability. International multilaboratory collaborations and dedicated consortia could develop shared guidelines. For fixed labels, this could involve establishing culturally informed vocabularies that systematically consider the nature (mentalistic/bodily, specific/general, positive/negative) of labels and their category representativeness. We acknowledge that label selection necessarily depends on study aims, but comparable lexical variability across studies remains important for consistent measurement. Likewise, for natural language approaches, validated language-and culture-specific lexicons balancing standardization with flexibility for contextual variation in emotional expression may reduce certain sources of bias.

Finally, we encourage interdisciplinary collaboration among psychologists, linguists, statisticians, and computational scientists via dedicated task forces, integrating quantitative and qualitative approaches. Natural language approaches, though underused, offer authentic, contextually grounded emotional expression, while standardized lexical resources offer comparability and reproducibility (Hoemann, Warfel, et al., 2025). Rather than viewing these approaches as competing alternatives, future research could seek to combine their complementary strengths within measurement designs that remain faithful to the construct's theoretical conceptualization. This may include, for example, combining self-report intensity ratings with computational analyses of openended emotional descriptions (e.g., using techniques such as word embeddings, contextual language models, and topic modeling) to yield more context-and process-sensitive measures of ED.

5. Conclusion

The present systematic review mapped how performance-based ED has been conceptualized and measured across 115 studies. The literature is unevenly distributed: It centers on dispositional, negative, and integral ED, while state-level, positive, global, and between-or within-category ED remain comparatively understudied. Operationalizations vary widely in measurement approach (ecological vs. nonecological), emotional vocabulary (predefined labels vs. natural language), and computation. Crucially, many methodological decisions that affect ED scores are inconsistently applied or not reported, and the limited convergence among indices suggests that they may not be interchangeable.

These findings indicate that heterogeneity in ED research is not only a technical matter, but rather, different operationalizations embody different assumptions about what counts as evidence of differentiation. Inconsistencies in the association between ED and psychological functioning may therefore stem partly from differences in what is measured, rather than solely from differences in the construct's adaptive value (Hong et al., 2025; Whiting & Nook, 2026).

To move the field forward, we recommend that researchers justify their conceptualization of ED and report methodological choices transparently. These are prerequisites for meta-analytic syntheses, which are needed to systematically evaluate how different methodological choices impact construct validity and identify best practices. Equally essential is a refinement of measurement that reflects the theoretical definition of ED more closely. By linking theoretical definitions, measurement strategies, and reporting standards, the field can build a more coherent and cumulative understanding of emotion differentiation.

Table S5. The screening process involved the following steps.

1. All identified study records were uploaded to the Rayyan platform (Ouzzani et al., 2016) and automatic deduplication procedures were applied. Two researchers independently performed a double-blind screening of titles and abstracts to determine the inclusion or exclusion of each record. Any disagreement was solved by involving a third reviewer, who facilitated the consensus process.

2. Full-text screening: The records that passed the initial screening were subjected to a doubleblind reading of their full texts. The assessment for inclusion or exclusion was based on predefined criteria, and the reasons for the decisions were documented. Disagreements were once again solved through discussion among the three researchers. Interrater agreement was calculated via Cohen's Kappa coefficient, with a k value of 0.70 or higher considered acceptable.

3. The reference list of all eligible articles was examined to identify additional studies that explicitly mentioned the constructs "emotion differentiation" or "emotional granularity". The same screening process (title and abstract screening, full-text review, and conflict resolution) was applied to these newly identified studies.

1.2. Data Extraction

For each eligible study, data extraction was carried out by two independent reviewers through a two-step process including an extraction and a verification stage. In the extraction stage, the first reviewer recorded the following information: metadata (citation details, corresponding author's contact information), methodological details, sample characteristics, study objectives, and main findings regarding ED correlates. Details regarding the information included in each category are displayed in Table S1.

During the verification stage, the second reviewer independently cross-checked all the extracted data to ensure accuracy and consistency. In cases of discrepancies between the two reviewers, a second round of independent extractions was conducted.

1.3. Synthesis

Due to the heterogeneity of the study designs and methodologies in the field, we employed a narrative synthesis approach to integrate findings across studies. Employing a deductive thematic analysis approach (Braun & Clarke, 2006), the final synthesis combined all the components into a structured and coherent narrative. The findings are reported thematically and supported by summary tables to enhance clarity and comparability across studies.

(2018) Emotion experience (1) Divergent patterns of affect labeling relate most strongly to difficulty identifying feelings (2) ED and dialecticism relate most strongly to difficulty describing feelings Quasiexperimental Sample size: n = 108 Population: undergraduates Age: M(SD) = 19.3(0.88) Sex/gender: 67.6% women Correlational analysis: correlation between negative ED and alexithymia (-) * , affect labeling (+) * , intensity of primary emotions (-), arousal (-), negative dialectism (+), positive dialectism (+); correlation between positive ED and alexithymia (-), affect labeling (-), intensity of primary emotions (+), arousal (-), negative dialectism (+), positive dialectism (+) Regression analysis: negative ED predicts difficulty describing feelings (-) * but not difficulty identifying feelings (-); positive ED does not predict difficulty identifying feelings (-) nor externally-oriented thinking (+) 2. (2001) Emotion experience (1) Individuals with high ED have better ER than individuals with poor ED (2) This effect is stronger for negative emotional experience Longitudinal intensive Sample size: n = 53 Population: // Age: M (SD) = // Sex/gender: 19 men Moderation analysis: negative ED is related to negative ER (+) ** , particularly at higher levels of emotional intensity (+) * ; neither positive ED (+) nor its interaction with emotional intensity (-) are related to positive ER 3. Berman et al. (2024) Emotion experience (1) Qualitatively distinct ED states based on state-specific measurement models of emotion ratings can be identified using LMFA (2) Momentary stress is related to the probability of transitioning between ED states (3) Individuals differ in the transitions between ED states (4) Neuroticism and dispositional mood regulation (negative mood repair and positive mood maintenance) predict latent class membership of individuals who Longitudinal intensive Sample size: n = 139 Population: university students and general population Age: M(SD) = 30.52(9.03) Sex/gender: 81% female, 17% male, 2% nonbinary LMFA (identifying latent ED states): three latent ED states for the negative emotions (State1 = High negative intensity, low ED; State2 = Low ED between anger and sadness: State3 = High ED between anger and sadness) and three for the positive emotions (State1 = High positive intensity, high ED; State2 = high ED between love, joy, and confidence; State3 = High positive intensity, high ED)

LMFA (momentary stress as a predictor of transitions between ED states): higher momentary stress is associated with a higher probability of transitioning from the "high ED between anger and sadness" state to the "high negative intensity, low ED" and "low ED between anger and sadness" states and a lower probability of differ in transitions between ED states transitioning from the "high negative intensity, low ED" and "low ED between anger and sadness" states to the "high ED between anger and sadness" state MIXTURE LMFA (identifying and predicting latent classes of individuals who differ in state transitions): Class C1_neg is characterized by lower probabilities of remaining in a particular state than Class C2_neg. Class C2_neg showed a very high overall probability of transitioning to or remaining in the "high negative intensity, low ED" state, a low to moderately high probability of transitioning to or remaining in the "low ED between anger and sadness" state, and low probabilities of transitioning to or remaining in the "high ED between anger and sadness" and "no negative emotions" states. Each between-person covariate significantly predicts class membership. Individuals with low neuroticism scores has a very high probability of being in the "variability in negative ED" class, but this probability decreases as neuroticism increases (while the probability of being in the "high negative intensity, low ED" class increases). In contrast, individuals with low scores on negative mood repair or positive mood maintenance have high probabilities of being in the "high negative intensity, low ED" class, and these probabilities decrease as scores on either of these variables increase 83.
