Blameworthy 4 Confident 3 --2.5. Table S5. Recommendations for Future Research on Emotion Differentiation, Both in Terms of Measurement Options and Reporting Requirements Table S5. Recommendations for future research on Emotion Differentiation, both in terms of measurement options and reporting requirements. Area of Analysis Dimension of Analysis Operationalization and Methodological Choices Reporting Requirements Conceptualization Temporal framing  Dispositional ED  Daily ED  Momentary ED Studies should justify whether ED is conceptualized and measured as a dispositional trait or a state-level (i.e., daily, momentary) construct. The choice of temporal framing should be theoretically motivated and aligned with the research question. Emotional Valence  Positive ED  Negative ED  Global ED Authors should report whether ED is examined for positive emotions, negative emotions, or globally across valences. The rationale for focusing on a specific valence (or combining valences) should be explicitly stated. Emotional Category  Integral ED  Between-category ED  Within-category ED Researchers should clarify whether ED is assessed as integral (across all emotions), betweencategory (across different emotion families), or within-category (within the same emotion family). Authors should discuss whether and how distinguishing among emotion categories adds theoretical or empirical value relative to the study aims or justify why such distinctions are not considered.

Emotion Vocabulary

Fixed Emotion Labels

Valence of Labels  Positive  Negative  Neutral

The valence of the selected emotion labels (positive, negative, neutral) should correspond to the valence specified in the conceptualization of ED. Particular attention should be paid to labels that may carry both positive and negative connotations depending on context.

Type of Labels  Degree of Specificity  Bodily, Mental, Cognitive Connotations Authors should describe the criteria used to select emotion labels. The labels set should be appropriate for the research objectives, sufficiently broad to capture subtle emotional distinctions, and representative across different levels of emotional experience. Studies should report whether participants were given the option to select an "other" category and/or  Representativeness of Emotion Categories to self-generate emotion labels if none of the provided options adequately captured their experience.

No. of Labels -The rationale for the number of emotion labels included should be reported. Authors should clarify whether a variable number of emotion terms was used to represent emotion categories within or across emotion families. When both positive and negative valences are examined, comparability in the number of labels across valences should be addressed.

Intensity Rating  Slider Scale  Likert Scale

The method used to assess emotional intensity (e.g., Slider Scale, Likert Scale), along with the number of scale points or intervals, should be specified.

Emotion Vocabulary

Natural Language

Format  Open-ended Narratives  Freely Generated Labels Authors should report whether emotional language was collected via open-ended narratives or freely generated emotion labels. Instructions provided to participants should be described and evaluated for consistency with the declared ED conceptualization (e.g., the temporal frame of reference).

Emotion Lexicon Identification

 Relying on Existing Lexicons  Relying on Criteria Defined by the Authors

Researchers should specify whether emotion words were identified using existing lexicons or criteria defined by the authors. When author-defined criteria are used, these criteria should be explicitly articulated and described in full; in such cases, inter-judge agreement procedures should be preferred.

Criteria for Valence Classification

 Relying on Existing Lexicons  Relying on Criteria Defined by the Authors  Self-report Valence

Rating by the Participants

The criteria for classifying emotion words as positively or negatively valenced should be clearly stated, including existing lexicons, participant self-reporting, or author-defined criteria. In this latter case, inter-judge agreement procedures should be employed.

Intensity of Emotion Lexicon

Studies should indicate whether and how emotional intensity was evaluated in natural language data. This may include participant-rated intensity of generated emotion words (e.g., using Slider or Likert Scales) or linguistic markers such as modifiers (e.g., adverbs, adjectives).

Criteria for Emotion Lexicon Classification

 Relying on Existing Lexicons

Authors should describe the coding procedures used to classify emotion-related terms as specific, basic, or general for ED scoring. Inter-judge agreement should be reported when classification criteria are defined by the authors.

 Relying on Criteria Defined by the Authors

Use of Paraphrased or Metaphorical Language

Researchers should state whether paraphrased or metaphorical emotional language was considered in ED assessment. If so, criteria for its identification, interpretation, and classification should be specified.

Measurement Approach Ecological: ESM EMA  Days  Prompts per Day  Frequency  Temporal Frame of Reference Authors should report the duration of the EMA period, whether days were consecutive, the number of prompts per day, and prompt timing (random, semi-random, or fixed). The daily time window for assessments should be specified, along with the temporal frame of reference for emotional reports (e.g., in-the-moment, since last prompt). Justification should be provided for whether the number of daily prompts adequately captures emotional experience relative to the research question. Inclusion criteria for participant compliance (e.g., minimum number of completed prompts) should be clearly described and justified. Diary  Days  Frequency  Moment of the Day  Temporal Frame of Reference Studies should report the total duration, assessment frequency (e.g., daily, weekly), and time of day of diary completion. The temporal anchoring of emotional reports (e.g., entire day/week, specific emotional episode) should be specified. Criteria for participant inclusion based on completed entries should be illustrated and motivated. DRM  Days  Frequency  Episodes  Moment of the Day  Temporal Frame of Reference Authors should indicate the duration of DRM administration, assessment frequency, number of episodes reconstructed per day, and timing of completion. The temporal frame of reference for emotional reports (e.g., same day, previous day) should be specified.

Event-contingent  Sampled Events

Researchers should describe the types of emotional events sampled and justify their relevance to the study aims. Criteria used to limit between-person variability in the number and characterization of sampled events should be reported.

Measurement Approach

Non-ecological: ED Task Setting  Laboratory  Online

The administration context (laboratory vs. online) should be specified. For laboratory studies, procedures to reduce social desirability bias should be described. For online studies, steps taken to standardize and control the testing environment should be reported.

Stimuli  Type  Valence  Number  Temporal Frame of Reference Authors should describe the type of stimuli used, as well as the criteria guiding stimulus selection and the instructions provided at the time of administration. The use of standardized and validated stimuli should be reported, along with standardization procedures if nonvalidated stimuli are used. Authors should clarify whether stimulus valence can be determined a priori. The number of stimuli and trials administered should be declared and justified. It should be specified whether tasks involve immediate responses to in-the-moment emotion-eliciting stimuli or reflective evaluations of past autobiographical events.

ED Index Computation

Relying on Fixed Labels

The method used to compute the ED index should be specified (e.g., ICC-based, AIC-based, PCA-based, PROC VARCOMP). For ICC-based approaches, authors should report whether absolute agreement or consistency was estimated and how negative ICC values were handled (e.g., coded as zero, treated as missing).

Handling of Zerovariance Cases

 Excluded  Recoded Authors should describe how zero-variance cases were managed. For dispositional ED, procedures for handling measurement occasions with no variance should be reported. For state-level ED computed, the treatment of zero-variance cases in numerators or denominators should be clearly specified.

Grouping of Emotion Labels

 Global ED  Between-and Withincategory ED For global ED, authors should clarify whether positive and negative ED indices were computed separately and then averaged, or whether all labels were used simultaneously. Differences in results across methods should be reported if relevant. For within-and between-category ED, the grouping procedure and exact computational steps should be explicitly described.

ED Index Computation

Relying on Natural Language

Method  Emotion Lexicon Classification  Computational Procedure Authors should specify which emotion lexicon categories (e.g., specific, basic, general) were defined and which computational procedures were used to derive ED indices (e.g., SI, NS).

Grouping of Emotion Labels

 Global ED  Between-and Withincategory ED Authors should report whether global ED was computed by averaging valence-specific indices or by pooling all emotion terms, and whether results differ across methods. Procedures for computing within-and between-category ED should be described in detail.

different operationalizations may capture partially distinct aspects of what is theoretically understood as ED, arguably reflecting alternative notions of what it means to differentiate emotions. The linguistic representations collected during assessment and the procedures used to quantify and interpret relationships among emotion words embody different interpretations of how the underlying theoretical assumptions should be translated into measurable indicators. Establishing validity therefore requires not only evaluating the statistical properties of an ED index but also examining the correspondence between the theoretical meaning of differentiation, the information collected to assess it, and the assumptions through which that information is translated into an observed ED score.

For ecological methods (EMA, diary, DRM, event-contingent protocols), reporting should include detailed sampling characteristics, such as assessment duration, frequency, timing, temporal reference, and compliance criteria. Similarly, for non-ecological ED tasks, clear reporting should cover testing setting, stimulus characteristics, instructions, number of trials, and temporal reference guiding participants' judgment.Third, greater care is needed in selecting and describing emotional vocabulary. For fixed labels, it is recommended to include a sufficiently broad, representative set across emotion categories and report selection criteria (valence, specificity, semantic content against domain representativeness), label distribution across valences and categories, and availability of alternative responses (e.g., "other" option along with self-generated labels). For natural language approaches, authors should provide detailed information on the criteria and procedures used to identify and code emotional terms, including the classification of emotional versus non-emotional language, determination of valence and specificity, and treatment of metaphorical or paraphrased expressions.Finally, studies should describe the statistical procedures used to derive ED indices and share codes as open materials to allow reproducibility and transparency of computational methods, aligning with open science practices and recommendations. For computation strategies relying on label ratings, handling of zero-variance cases and procedures to derive global, between-and within-category ED should be reported in detail. When computing ICC-based indices, researchers should report the decisions regarding the ICC method (consistency, agreement) and treatment of negative ICC values.

Emotional labels, divided by valence, are presented in descending order of frequency, from the most to the least frequently used. ° indicates affective labels categorized as generic (i.e., non-specific). * indicates affective labels categorized as bodily (i.e., non-mentalistic). The classification of labels (specific vs. generic; mentalistic vs. bodily) was performed using the Johnson-Laird and Oatley (1989) corpus in conjunction with inter-rater agreement; although conducted as rigorously as possible, this classification remains inherently arbitrary and may be subject to bias.3.
